artifacts.notes: This is a transcription of a web witness of the 1895 printing, not a collation against the printed page, so no passage taken from it rises above inspected. It supersedes the earlier basil-hexaemeron-1-web-text-0823184f, which held Homily I alone and was assembled by hand from two model-mediated readings. Collating that file against these bytes found two defects in it that the route it used could not have shown: an entire paragraph of section 5 was missing, beginning “The first movement is called beginning”, and two further paragraphs had been run together into one. The earlier file also read “according heaven the privilege of seniority” where this witness reads “according to heaven”; that one is a genuine divergence between readings rather than a defect in either, and it stands open against the printed page along with the three divergences the earlier record listed.

passages.context: The whole of the first Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 16 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.”. The first homily reaches no verse beyond its lemma: it expounds the word beginning in its several senses and the naming of the two extremes, and the second day is not reached until Homily III opens by saying so.

passages.context: The whole of the second Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 21 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “The earth was invisible and unfinished.”. The lemma is Genesis 1:2 in the Septuagint reading. The homily runs on through the Spirit borne upon the waters, the making of light and its division from the darkness, and closes in section 8 on “and the evening and the morning were one day”, which is Genesis 1:5.

passages.context: The whole of the third Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 17 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “On the firmament.”. Section 1 states that the works of the first day have been recounted and that this is the second day. The homily expounds “let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters” and closes on the firmament being called Heaven. The recollection of the light of Genesis 1:3 is a back-reference and does not widen the extent.

passages.context: The whole of the fourth Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 14 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “Upon the gathering together of the waters.”. Section 2 opens on “let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear” and the homily runs to the naming of the dry land Earth and the gathering of waters Seas. The reference back to the invisible earth of Genesis 1:2 is a recollection, not an exposition.

passages.context: The whole of the ninth Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 16 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “The creation of terrestrial animals.”. Section 2 expounds “let the earth bring forth the living creature” and section 6 reaches “and God said let us make man”, where the series breaks off: Basil defers the creation of man to another discourse and the ninth homily is the last. Genesis 1:26 is therefore the furthest verse the whole Hexaemeron reaches.

passages.context: The whole of the fifth Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 17 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “The germination of the earth.”. Every section quotes and expounds one lemma, “let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself”, which is Genesis 1:11. The homily nowhere quotes the earth's obedience in 1:12 or the closing of the third day in 1:13, so the extent is not widened to them.

passages.context: The whole of the sixth Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 25 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “The creation of luminous bodies.”. Section 2 opens on “let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, and to divide the day from the night” and section 9 on “and God made two great lights”, which are Genesis 1:14 and 1:16. The light of the first day is recalled only as the premise that the luminaries are not that light.

passages.context: The whole of the eighth Hexaemeron homily, preached at Caesarea in Lent 378, in all 20 of the paragraphs the printing gives it. Its lemma is “The creation of fowl and water animals.”. This homily genuinely spans two days' commands. Section 1 opens on “let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle and creeping things, and beast of the earth after his kind”, which is Genesis 1:24, and then turns back to ask why the waters received one command and the earth another; sections 2, 7 and 8 expound “let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life and fowl that may fly above the earth”, which is Genesis 1:20. The extent therefore runs from 1:20 to 1:24 and is not narrowed to the homily's title.

work.author: Philip Schaff and Henry Wace
work.description: The eighth volume of the second series of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation anthology, containing Basil of Caesarea's letters, the Hexaemeron, and On the Spirit in English, with the volume editors' prolegomena. Its container identity remains distinct from Basil's own works printed within it.
